query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the particle velocity during HVAF-i7 deposition by adjusting the fuel/oxygen ratio will improve deposition efficiency and overcome the thickness limitation, yielding a thicker, adherent FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy bond coat with controlled as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a 15–45 μm feedstock produced via gas atomization, previously used with standard HVAF-i7 parameters yielding acceptable quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.intervention: Modify the HVAF-i7 torch parameters—specifically increase the fuel/oxygen ratio (for example, increasing oxygen flow relative to fuel)—to boost particle velocity during deposition.
generation.conditions: Deposition performed on standard structural bond-coat substrates under typical spray distances (near 300–350 mm as found optimal in similar MCrAlY studies) and applicable to internal diameters as small as 120 mm; similar thermal and substrate pre-treatment conditions as prior experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy leads to improved impact dynamics and splat formation, which facilitates greater inter-splat bonding and film build-up.
generation.mechanism: The increased particle velocity reduces the time particles spend in the high-oxidation environment and improves their momentum on impact, resulting in a thicker coating with maintained adhesion and minimal excessive oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline using standard HVAF-i7 parameters with 15–45 μm feedstock, the intervention will yield coatings with significantly increased thickness while retaining acceptable oxidation levels and adhesion properties.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced with a 15–45 μm feedstock using standard HVAF-i7 parameters, which resulted in acceptable coating quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is expected under conditions similar to those used in prior studies—namely, with the same feedstock, optimized spray distances, and substrate geometries. Its benefits may be limited if excessive increases in oxygen flow lead to unintended oxidation or if other spray dynamics in restricted areas (like 120 mm diameters) are adversely affected.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the thickness increase and the balance between improved deposition efficiency and any potential increase in oxidation remain to be quantified. There is also uncertainty regarding the interplay between increased particle velocity and deposition quality in highly confined geometries.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform two sets of HVAF-i7 depositions using identical substrates and 15–45 μm FeCoNiCrAl feedstock. In one set, use the standard fuel/oxygen ratio; in the second set, adjust the torch parameters to increase particle velocity (by increasing the oxygen flow). Evaluate the coating thickness, adhesion, and oxidation levels.
measurements: Adhesion strength (via pull-off or scratch tests)
Oxidation levels (via XRD and EDS analysis)
In-flight particle velocity (using appropriate diagnostic methods)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the adjusted parameters do not lead to a statistically significant increase in coating thickness without compromising adhesion or exceeding acceptable oxidation levels, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). It is known [] that when Al concentration in FeCoNiCrAlMo0.5 is lower than 10%, FCC solid solution becomes preferable to BCC.
